column4: The section reads earth and sky as the floor and roof of one furnished world; this ayah makes the earth a bed (فِرَاشًا) and the sky a building, stating that domestic architecture directly.

The section hears a tent in the raised sky, pegged mountains, and spread ground, and notes a thick rug of camel hair or wool; this ayah joins hide tents with wool, fur, and hair furnishings, making the room-world analogy materially exact.
The section asks people to look at how the sky was raised; this ayah likewise asks whether they have looked at the sky above, then names its building, adornment, and lack of fissures.
Where the section treats the sky as a raised roof made by a craftsman's gesture, this ayah says that God built the sky with power, supplying the construction half of the same room-world pair.
The section's level earth is also a laid carpet; this ayah says the earth was spread as a bed and praises its Maker as the excellent spreader.
The section emphasizes that raising and placing belong to one furnishing sequence; this ayah puts them side by side in the raised sky and the placed balance (رَفَعَهَا وَوَضَعَ الْمِيزَانَ).
The section moves from objects placed in a room to the earth laid out for living creatures; this ayah says that the earth itself was placed for all creatures.
The section's flattened earth is the spread floor of the world; this ayah asks whether God made the earth a resting bed (مِهَادًا).
The prose defines mountains as the earth's great pegs; this ayah states the same domestic-cosmic image by calling the mountains pegs (أَوْتَادًا).
The section treats the sky as a constructed roof; this ayah asks whether human creation is harder or the sky which God built, beginning the construction sequence continued in 79:28-32.
The section cites the raised sky as a ceiling made even; this ayah names both acts, raising its canopy and proportioning it (رَفَعَ سَمْكَهَا فَسَوَّاهَا).
In the sequence begun at 79:27, this ayah adds the earth spread out after the sky, matching the section's movement from raised ceiling to laid ground.
In the same construction sequence, this ayah says God anchored the mountains, matching the section's mountains erected as the world's pegs.
The section hears architecture in the raised sky; this oath names the sky and the One who built it, making construction the act by which the cosmos appears.
The section's last hand movement is making the earth an even spread; this oath names the earth and the One who spread it out.
The section turns the made world into a furnished space offered to sight; this ayah places constellations in the sky and adorns it for those who look.
The section imagines a tent-like world with a raised roof and discusses its pole; this ayah says God raised the heavens without visible pillars, directly marking the absent supports.
The prose defines the sky through a house roof; this ayah explicitly makes the sky a protected roof (سَقْفًا مَحْفُوظًا).
The section sees the world as a habitable room and creation as skilled shaping; this ayah makes earth a settled place, sky a building, and human forms beautiful in one account.
The section's earth is a rug-like spread beneath the world's tent; Noah tells his people here that God made the earth for them as a carpet (بِسَاطًا).
The room-world has a strong raised ceiling; this ayah describes seven strong structures built above its hearers.

The section joins a pillarless sky, set mountains, and creatures spread across earth; this ayah contains all three: heavens without visible pillars, firm mountains, and every creature broadcast on earth.
The prose explicitly links creation to broadcasting living beings over the made world; this ayah joins creation of the heavens and earth with the creatures God has spread through them.
The section hears مَبْثُوثَةٌ as both carpets spread and living beings broadcast on earth; this ayah places that broadcasting of every creature inside a detailed heavens-and-earth sign scene.

The section makes straight measure, an extended floor, and upright mountains aspects of one craft; this ayah joins earth spread out, firm mountains set in it, and everything grown there in due measure.
The section connects raised mountains and exact measure in making the world fit; this ayah sets firm mountains above the earth and measures its provisions.
The section's ground is spread and its mountains erected as fixed features; this ayah likewise joins earth extended with firm mountains cast into it.
The section develops خَلْق as straight and exact measuring before a thing is made; this ayah declares that every thing is created according to a measure.
The prose recovers measuring as the first act of creation; this ayah joins creating every thing to determining it with exact determination (فَقَدَّرَهُ تَقْدِيرًا).
The section explicitly invokes this formulation to ground all four making gestures in order: the Creator creates and then makes proportionate (خَلَقَ فَسَوَّىٰ).
The section explicitly extends its craft image to the human body; this ayah joins creating, proportioning, and balancing the addressee.
Like the section's sequence from creation to making straight, this ayah says that God created the human being and then proportioned him.
The prose explains creation through prior measurement; this ayah says that God created the human being from a drop and then determined his measure or course.
The section finds uprightness and right measure beneath creation; this ayah locates human creation in the finest configuration (أَحْسَنِ تَقْوِيمٍ).
The section asks the hearer to inspect a made sky and its even order; this ayah describes layered heavens with no disparity and commands the gaze to search for a fissure.
This ayah repeats the inspecting gaze begun in 67:3 until it returns defeated, turning the section's question about how things were made into a sustained test of their flawless measure.
The section commands attention to how the camel and world were created; this ayah commands travel through the earth and looking at how creation was begun.
The section's first world-object is the created camel and it speaks of a maker's hand movements; this ayah asks whether people see the livestock created for them by what God's hands made.
The section joins the camel with the straight row of cushions; this ayah brings those details together in sacrificial camels standing in orderly rows (صَوَافَّ).
The prose defines a row as placing things on one straight line and repeatedly compares furnishing to building; this ayah combines both images in a rank like a compact structure.

The prose explicitly derives صَفْصَف from the straight row and applies it to level land; after 20:105 removes the mountains, this ayah leaves the ground a bare level plain (قَاعًا صَفْصَفًا), a Last-Day reversal of the furnished world.
The section explains رفع as raising a construction; this ayah shows Abraham and Ishmael raising the foundations of the House, a literal building use of the same gesture.
Placed cups become part of a larger account of things and spaces set down for inhabitants; this ayah calls the first House the one placed (وُضِعَ) for humankind.
The section has raised couches; this ayah performs the closely corresponding action when Joseph raises his parents onto the throne, joining physical elevation to furnished seating.
The section notes that رفع is used for building upward; this ayah speaks of houses God permitted to be raised, while its context also permits the sense of honoring them.
The section's raised furniture opens onto an architectural Garden; this ayah promises chambers above which are further chambers, all built, giving vertical form to the prepared dwelling.
The section explicitly hears the sky as the roof of a house; this oath to the raised roof (السَّقْفِ الْمَرْفُوعِ) condenses that cosmic architecture.
The section's Garden room contains couches and a straight row; this ayah reunites the same details in couches set in rows (سُرُرٍ مَصْفُوفَةٍ) on which the blessed recline.
The section's couches are raised; this ayah gives the nearest Garden furnishing parallel in raised beds (فُرُشٍ مَرْفُوعَةٍ).
The section's room is arranged for repose; this ayah places the Garden's purified companions as brothers on couches facing one another.
The prepared room becomes inhabited here: Garden-dwellers recline on couches amid flowing rivers, showing the use of the seating listed in the section.
The section lists the still furnishings of a Garden room; this ayah places the Garden-dwellers and their spouses reclining on couches in shade.
The section's raised couches form a social room; this ayah seats the honored servants on couches facing one another.
The Garden's couches and the world's furnished rooms meet here in doors and couches made for unbelievers' houses; 43:35 limits all of it to temporary worldly enjoyment.
The section's array of Garden furnishings is matched by this scene of reclining on beds whose inner linings are brocade, adding the tactile construction of the bedding.
The section ends its room-list with spread carpets and cushions; this ayah seats the Garden-dwellers on green cushions or spreads and beautiful carpets.
The section's elevated seating belongs to an ordered Garden interior; this ayah introduces elaborately woven or arrayed couches.
This ayah supplies the posture and relation for the couches named in 56:15: the blessed recline on them facing one another, as in the section's prepared room.
The section's furnished Garden room is a place of rest; this ayah places its people reclining there on couches, sheltered from harsh sun and cold.
The section moves from looking at creation to raised Garden seating; this ayah unites repose and vision as the righteous look out from couches.
This repeated scene again has the blessed looking from couches, echoing both the section's furnishing and its command to see what has been made.
The section has cups already placed in the Garden room; here a cup from a flowing spring is circulated among the reclining blessed, showing that prepared vessel in use.
The section's placed cups become active hospitality here as golden trays and cups are circulated around the Garden-dwellers.
The section supplies cups as part of the room; this ayah shows the inhabitants passing a cup among one another without the corrupting speech or sin of earthly drinking.
The section's cups are set ready; this ayah introduces immortal youths circulating among the blessed, and 56:18 names the vessels they carry.
Continuing 56:17, this ayah names goblets, pitchers, and a cup from a flowing spring, closely expanding the section's single placed-cup image.
The section describes cups set in an ordered room; this ayah has silver vessels and crystal cups circulated around the Garden-dwellers.
The prose says the maker's work begins in exact measure; this ayah describes the Garden's silver crystal vessels as measured with precise measure (قَدَّرُوهَا تَقْدِيرًا).
The section's placed cups belong to Garden provision; this ayah names a brimming cup within its parallel list of Garden rewards.
The section furnishes the Garden with raised seating and makes earth a bed beneath a roof; this ayah gives Hell a bed with coverings above, a direct infernal reversal of that habitable room.
The section's world depends on an elevated roof and upright construction; this ayah has God strike a building at its foundations so that its roof falls upon its makers.
The section fixes mountains upright over a spread earth; this ayah moves the mountains away and leaves the earth exposed, dismantling both parts of that arrangement.
The section's mountains are erected as the world's pegs; this ayah answers the question about them by saying God will pulverize them, preparing the level plain of 20:106.
After 20:105 removes the mountains and 20:106 leaves a level plain, this ayah says no curvature or unevenness will be seen there, completing the reversal of pegged, articulated terrain.
The section unfolds the sky as a high roof; this ayah folds that sky like a written scroll, reversing the gesture by which the world-room was opened and raised.

The section describes the world through a maker's hand movements; this ayah has the whole earth grasped and the heavens folded in God's right hand on the Last Day, an answering gesture of dismantling.
The section's erected mountains seem to be the fixed workmanship of the world; this ayah says they appear rigid yet pass like clouds, while naming God's craft that perfects every thing.
After 43:33-34 imagine silver roofs, stairs, doors, and couches, this ayah calls all such furnishing only the enjoyment of the nearer life and reserves the final abode for the reverent.
The same surah swears by the raised roof in 52:5; this ayah shows the sky convulsing on the promised Day, undoing that stable ceiling.
Alongside the shaking sky of 52:9, the mountains move away here; the surah later answers that dismantled world with the lined Garden couches of 52:20.
Earlier this surah raises the sky and places the earth; here the sky is split and becomes rose-red like oil or hide, marking the end of the constructed canopy.
The section's raised furnishings and high Garden give elevation a physical form; this ayah calls the Event both abasing and raising, transferring the same vertical opposition to final destinies.
The section erects mountains as stable pegs; this ayah crushes them completely, and 56:6 turns their remains into dispersed dust.
The section's carpets are مَبْثُوثَةٌ in orderly abundance; after the mountains are crushed in 56:5, this ayah makes them scattered dust (هَبَاءً مُنْبَثًّا), reversing furnishing into dispersal.
The section composes earth and mountains as floor and pegs; this ayah has both carried up and crushed with one crushing, undoing the assembled pair together.
The section's sky is a raised, stable roof; this ayah says the sky will split and become frail on that Day, reversing both its integrity and strength.
The section connects mountains with rugs and wool through the world's furnishings; this ayah turns the mountains into tufts of wool, dissolving rigid pegs into textile-like matter.
The section's upright mountains peg a level earth; this ayah makes earth and mountains quake until the mountains become a loose heap of sand.
The section raises the sky as an intact canopy; this ayah marks the promised Day by that sky being opened or rent apart.
The section's mountains are deliberately set upright; this ayah marks the promised Day by their being uprooted and blown away.
Within the same surah that calls the mountains pegs in 78:7, this ayah makes them move away until they are a mirage, explicitly reversing their apparent stability.
The section asks how mountains were erected; this ayah marks the Last Day by their being set in motion, the opposite of fixed upright placement.
The section reads the sky as the roof covering the world-room; this ayah has that covering stripped away.
The section's raised sky forms a whole ceiling; this ayah opens the Last-Day scene with that sky split apart.
The section sees the sky as a raised, intact ceiling; this ayah opens the final scene with that sky split apart, before 84:3 stretches out the earth below.
The section's earth is deliberately leveled as the world's floor; in the scene begun at 84:1, this ayah stretches it out at the Judgment, a final and destructive counterpart to its first preparation.
The prose explicitly contrasts carpets spread in the Garden with people scattered on that Day; this ayah makes the people like dispersed moths (الْفَرَاشِ الْمَبْثُوثِ).
Beside the dispersed people of 101:4, the erected mountains become carded wool here; the world's pegs turn into the same soft textile register as its rugs.
The section's world is made by spreading ground and fixing mountains into it; this ayah joins the extended earth with firm mountains, rivers, and paired fruits.
The prose treats mountains as planted pegs that make the earth fit; this ayah says God cast firm mountains into earth so that it would not sway with its inhabitants.
The section erects mountains within a stable floor; this ayah places firm mountains in earth so it will not shake with people, explaining a function of the pegs.
After 16:80 gives hide tents and animal-hair furnishings, this ayah gives shade and shelters in the mountains, extending the made world's protection from room to landscape.
The section reads land, mountains, and a made dwelling together; this ayah makes earth a stable abode and gives it rivers, firm mountains, and a barrier between seas.
The section's flattened earth is made usable for its inhabitants; this ayah calls the earth tractable and invites people to walk its reaches and eat its provision.
The section makes earth the containing floor of the common dwelling; this ayah asks whether God made it a gathering container, with 77:26 specifying the living and dead whom it contains.
After 77:25-26 makes earth a container, this ayah places lofty firm mountains in it and gives fresh water, another compact floor-and-pegs construction.
The section's earth is a laid and livable surface; this ayah says God made it a cradle or bed for people and traced roads through it.
Like the section's prepared ground, this ayah makes earth a cradle or bed for its addressees and places paths in it for guidance.
The section pairs furnishing the earth with proportioning the high sky; this ayah first provides all that is on earth and then forms the heavens into seven.
Following the sky's submission to shaping in 41:11, this ayah orders it as seven heavens and adorns the nearest one with lamps, adding furnishing to construction.
The section moves from a made room to a made sky; this ayah describes the nearest sky as adorned with stars, a cosmic counterpart to furnishing an interior.
After the measured layered heavens of 67:3, this ayah says the nearest heaven was adorned with lamps, showing the raised canopy also furnished with light.
The section asks people to look at how the sky was raised; Noah likewise asks whether they have seen how God created seven heavens in layers.
The section's command to look moves across camel, sky, mountains, and earth; this ayah commands people to look at what is in the heavens and earth, giving the same stance its widest field.

The section begins the made world with the camel and later hears rugs of hair and wool; this ayah says God created livestock for warmth, benefits, and food, supplying the animal material side of that craft.
After 36:71 calls livestock a work made for humans, this ayah says God subjected them so some are mounts and some food, answering in part what their created form is fitted to do.
The section's craft depends on right measure and a prepared earth; this ayah sends water down in measure and settles it in the earth, joining measurement to placement in the world.
The prose treats creation as competent, straight workmanship; this ayah says God made excellent every thing He created, stating the quality implied by the four careful gestures.
The section joins the true construction of heavens and earth to the proportioning of creatures; this ayah creates both in truth and then forms human beings beautifully.
The placed balance in 55:7 extends the section's right measure into conduct; this ayah makes the consequence explicit by forbidding transgression in the balance.
The section roots making in straight measure; this ayah commands establishing weight with justice and not making the balance deficient, turning crafted evenness into moral evenness.
The section links the act of placing with measure through the placed balance; this ayah places just balances for the Resurrection, extending that ordered gesture to exact judgment.
The prose's world resembles a tent while its room belongs to the Garden; this ayah places secluded companions in Garden tents, bringing the two spatial images together.
The section's cups are part of the Garden's prepared hospitality; this ayah says the righteous drink from a cup whose mixture is camphor, specifying what such a vessel bears.
The section's placed cup is here filled with a ginger mixture and served in the Garden, another concrete use of the prepared vessel.
The prose uses بث for both spreading rugs and spreading creatures; this ayah uses the same act for broadcasting many men and women from one pair across the human world.
The section connects a created creature with living beings spread through the world; this ayah makes both human creation and the creatures God continually disperses signs for certainty.
The prose defines صف as setting things on one straight line; this ayah presents humanity before its Lord in a row, applying the same arrangement to persons rather than cushions.
The cushions' صف is an orderly line; this oath by those ranged in ranks transfers that exact spatial order to a living host.
The section's straight arrangement of furnishings has a living counterpart here, where the angels say that they themselves are those who stand in ordered rows.
The section joins looking, sky, and straight arrangement; this ayah asks whether people see the birds above them with wings spread (صَافَّاتٍ), a mobile aerial use of the same root.
The section's line arranges the room; this ayah arranges the Spirit and angels standing in a row on the Day, shifting the same straight order to the heavenly assembly.
The repeated phrase row upon row (صَفًّا صَفًّا) makes the angelic arrival an ordered array, a solemn counterpart to the section's repeated arrangement of objects.

The section defines نصب as setting a protruding object upright and applies it to God's mountains; this ayah condemns humanly erected cult stones (الْأَنْصَابُ), a contrary use of the physical gesture.
The prose's نصب is an upright set object; this ayah likens people rushing from graves to a marker or cult-stone toward which they race, preserving that concrete set-up sense in a different scene.
The section treats upright setting as a builder's action; this ayah has the servant straighten or restore a wall about to collapse, a small-scale instance of making structure stand.
The world-image gives sky and mountain distinct jobs as roof and peg; this ayah raises Mount above the covenant people, making the mountain occupy the canopy's position.
As in 2:63, Mount is raised over the people; that exceptional scene reverses the section's normal arrangement of mountain fixed below and sky raised above.
This ayah repeats the covenant scene in which Mount is raised over the people, again placing the mountain where the section normally places the canopy.
The section's mountains are upright pegs beneath a roof; this ayah raises the mountain above the people like a canopy, deliberately exchanging the two cosmic roles.
The section asks how the sky stays raised as the world's roof; this ayah says God holds the sky back from falling upon earth except by permission.
The constructed world in the section depends on sustained placement; this ayah says God holds the heavens and earth lest they cease or slip away.
Immediately before the oath by the raised roof in 52:5, this ayah swears by the inhabited House, sharpening the section's reading of that roof as part of a dwelling.
